A-21 ACCESS AND AFFORDABILITY The University has developed a comprehensive enrollment management approach to foster access and affordability while also enhancing selectivity, quality, and student success.
These efforts include, but are not limited to, expansive recruitment strategies, predictive modeling, and an investment in financial aid.
These efforts have resulted in record applications and strong enrollments over the past 10 years, with a minor decline in new students that happened during the new FAFSA roll-out in Fall 2024.
A quick rebound in new student enrollment occurred for Fall 2025.
Student diversity, selectivity and quality have all improved each year.
Because of the University’s mission, the admissions policy is "selective" in that only students deemed prepared for university-level study are granted regular admission.
Due to Rhode Island’s size and declining number of high school graduates, the University enrolls a significant number of students from outside of Rhode Island.
Feedback from families that choose URI is that the University offers quality programs in a safe location at a good cost and value.

As part of the drive for accessibility and affordability, and recognizing the increasing educational diversity of potential students, the University maintains several programs for special populations and has started several new initiatives as well.
The University has worked to keep its tuition and fee rates affordable and competitive.
In addition to its traditional menu of financial aid programs, the University has the following special programs aimed at increasing access and affordability: Talent Development The Talent Development Program (“TD”) recruits and serves Rhode Island high school graduates with college potential who come from historically disadvantaged backgrounds.
Students admitted to TD have taken the required core academic courses in high school.
However, the average academic profile for students accepted to the TD program is not the average academic profile for students accepted through the regular admission process.
TD requires an intensive summer academic program prior to the start of the fall semester.
During the TD Summer Program students take university courses and live on campus.

TD students who successfully complete the TD Summer Program continue their enrollment at URI in the fall.
TD students receive academic and individual support from TD Advisors and mentors, and most receive the need based Hardge/Forleo Grant.
To be considered for the TD Program, students apply for admission to URI indicating their interest in TD, and then are considered through a competitive review process.

A-22 Academic Enhancement Center Part of the newly established Fannon Institute for Student Success, the Academic Enhancement Center (“AEC”) supports student learning and academic success through scaffolding student engagement with course content, helping with the development of metacogni tive strategies and skills, critical thinking, writing, time management, and test taking skills.
AEC programs are primarily peer -to-peer, enabling the Center to support the development of collaborative learning skills for all students, as well as teaching and leadership skills for student staff.
The AEC offers unique resources including three forms of tutoring in the STEM disciplines; an Academic Skills Development programming, including UCS 160; and the Writing Center for helping students at all levels of writing skills development.
The mission of the Academic Enhancement Center is to help students invest in their academic success.
The AEC learning support programs and services empower students to become more skillful and successful.

The AEC is committed to responding to student needs, collaborating with faculty and providing professional development for the student staff with the goal of enhancing student learning.
Pell Summer Promise Program In an effort to support Pell students in completing their education in a timely manner, URI launched the Pell Summer Promise Program using Federal Pell support and URI aid to help our most needy in -State students take free summer courses.
The goal is to en hance their time to degree and make college more affordable.
COMMUNITY, EQUITY AND DIVERSITY The Office of Community, Equity and Diversity leads institution -wide initiatives to anchor inclusion in every aspect of the University of Rhode Island’s community and operations.
To advance inclusive excellence, the Office convenes the University Diversity Council, with representatives from every University constituency; curates community education and development opportunities; conducts climate surveys; and, co-hosts with the Office of the President an annual Inclusive Excellence Awards ceremony recognizing faculty, student, staff and community partners’ efforts to foster an inclusive, people -centered culture.

In addition to coordinating the work of diversity professionals embedded in the University’s academic colleges and administrative divisions, the Office of Community, Equity and Diversity oversees four centers that host community development, engagement, ce lebration, and outreach programs for the entire University: Center for Military and Veteran Education The Center for Military and Veteran Education supports prior, present, and future military -connected students, faculty, and staff as they further their educational and professional objectives.
The Center assists in the transition from military life into student life and beyond and helps veterans connect with the resources and networks of support available to them at URI and within the local community.
Gender and Sexuality Center The URI Gender and Sexuality Center encourages students, faculty, and staff to explore and affirm their multiple and intersecting identities, especially surrounding gender and sexuality.
Through education, advocacy, and community -building, the Gender and S exuality Center strives to cultivate an inclusive campus culture that celebrates all genders and sexual identities.
The Center provides intersectional programming and collaborates with student leaders and campus partners to strengthen community and

A-23 foster belonging, all while nurturing a student -centered environment that supports academic and personal growth.
Multicultural Student Services Center The URI Multicultural Student Services Center is dedicated to developing a supportive and inclusive campus culture across the boundaries of culture, identity, and discipline.
Celebrating unity in diversity, the Multicultural Center invites all students, faculty, staff, administrators, alumni, and other friends to join in its work in creating a community of learners within and beyond URI.
The URI Multicultural Center collaboratively provides programs and resources that engage, connect and support the URI com munity in becoming just and culturally competent global citizens.
It also houses The Center for Nonviolence and Peace Studies which promotes and studies approaches to addressing conflict through nonviolence.
Women’s Center The URI Women’s Center partners with others in the URI community to provide an empowering space which promotes social justice for every member of the community, regardless of gender, gender identity, body, ability, sexual orientation, race, spirituality, a nd ethnicity.

Community members are encouraged to engage and foster continual dialogue on gender and issues that disproportionately affect women and their allies.
The URI Women’s Center supports all University students, faculty and staff in expanding their positive potential, agency and life experience.
STUDENT SERVICES Auxiliary Services Auxiliary services consist of housing, dining, student union, and health services which depend on restricted fees and related revenues derived from student clients.
These operations are required by State law to be fully self-supporting.
Undergraduate Housing On-campus residence halls are available to eligible students during the regular academic year and winter inter-session, with additional availability during the summer.
The University offers a variety of living accommodations with twenty seven residence hal ls and two apartment complexes.
The residence halls include twenty -two traditional residence halls, of which fifteen primarily house first -year residents in Living and Learning Communities, and three undergraduate apartment -style facilities, including the new Brookside apartment -style residence hall completed in January 2020.

There are also two International Engineering Program Houses managed by the College of Engineering.
First-year students are strongly encouraged to live on campus other than in exceptional circumstances; in the Fall of 2025 approximately 92% of URI first-year students live in residence halls.
During the Fall 2025 semester, 591 University students reside in the fraternity/sorority system which sponsors 16 sororities and fraternities (the “Greek” houses) located on university land but not owned or operated by the University.
The staff of the Office of Greek Life in the Memorial Union/Student Involvement Department advise these groups.
The Greek houses promote scholarship, citizenship and small group living.
Purchasing and business management for these houses is provided by a private non -profit corporation controlled by the fraternity and sorority members.
In additio n, students occupied two specialty houses for Engineering Students operated by the College of Engineering.
Another choice available to students is living "down the line" in rented rooms or houses near the University in the ocean-side resort areas.

For the Fall 2025 semester, 5,664 undergraduates were resident in on -campus (HRL) facilities on the Kingston campus.
Approximately 56% of URI undergraduate residents were first year students.
In Fall 2025, approximately 57% of undergraduates lived off campus in nearby communities or commuted from home.

Dining Centers Dining Services operates two all -you-care-to-eat facilities along with several retail locations across the Kingston Campus.

Counseling Services.
The Counseling Center is staffed by licensed mental health counselors, psychologists, and social workers.
The Center offers individual counseling and a variety of skill -building and support groups to help undergraduate and graduate students achieve their academic and life goals.
The Counseling Center provides assistance to students in areas such as adjusting to college life, coping with stress, building satisfying relationships, planning for the future, and coping with anxiety depression, substance use, or other mental health challenges.
The University partners with Telus Health to provide free, confidential, emotional health and wellbeing support, including access to clinicians 24/7 virtually, by phone or chat.
University Chaplains.

The chaplains work together to foster dialogue, understanding, and respect among people of different faiths and traditions.
Memorial Union.

Student Involvement staff are available to student leaders to provide advising and education in addition to assisting with the planning for their student organization’s events.

Health Services provides laboratory, radiology, and pharmacy services for URI students.

Violence Prevention and Advocacy Services are a part of the Health Services providing awareness, education, and support for survivors of sexual violence and Alcohol and other Drug Education provide comprehensive education, training and support on substance use and prevention.

The Dean of Students Office.

INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY SERVICES The University’s Information Technology Services organization (“ITS”) provides leadership, governance, and strategic direction for the technology and enterprise systems that support the University of Rhode Island community.
ITS is responsible for the relia bility, security, and ongoing modernization of systems that support instruction, research, administration, and daily University operations.
ITS supports core institutional systems used across the University, including the Learning Management System for online and in-person instruction; enterprise administrative systems supporting student records, human resources, and financial operations; and centralized support services through the University Help Desk.

ITS also operates and maintains the University’s high-speed network infrastructure, which connects URI campuses to one another and to national and global research networks through secure, multi -gigabit fiber-optic connectivity.
During the past year, the University expanded its research computing and artificial intelligence capabilities through the launch of the Institute for AI and Computational Research.
The Institute coordinates advanced computing, artificial intelligence, and data-intensive research activities across the University and strengthens URI’s participation at the Massachusetts Green High Performance Computing Center (MGHPCC), increasing available computing capacity, resilience, and access to shared regional infrastructure.
ITS provides artificial intelligence and research computing infrastructure not only for URI, but for nearly all public and private institutions of higher education in Rhode Island, excluding Brown University.
These services support the University of Rhode Island, Rhode Island College, Community College of Rhode Island, Bryant University, Salve Regina University, and other partner institutions.

This shared infrastructure model supports instruction, faculty research, and workforce development across the state and is provided to partner institutions at no cost.
To support the expanding use of artificial intelligence in teaching, research, and administrative functions, ITS launched a University -hosted AI platform based on LibreChat, deployed within a secure cloud environment.
The platform provides controlled acces s to multiple large language models hosted through

A-26 approved cloud providers and is designed to protect institutional and research data by isolating usage from public systems.
ITS has also deployed a secure version of Microsoft Copilot for all University faculty and staff, enabling productivity gains while maintaining institutional security and data governance standards.
Federal research sponsors increasingly require higher levels of data protection and compliance.
In response, ITS partnered with Hermathena Labs to provide secure research computing environments compliant with National Institute of Standards and Technology Special Publication 800-171 and Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification requirements.
In parallel, the University is developing its own higher-security research enclave, known as Sanctuary, at MGHPCC.
Sanctuary is intended to provide a University -controlled environment for sensitive, regulated, and export -controlled research workloads, expanding long -term institutional capacity and reducing reliance on third-party platforms as resources permit.
Cybersecurity remains a significant and evolving challenge for higher education.

ITS has continued to strengthen the University’s security posture through expanded use of multi-factor authentication, enhanced network monitoring and intrusion prevention cap abilities, and continued investment in disaster recovery and ransomware resilience.
These efforts are designed to reduce operational risk, protect sensitive information, and ensure continuity of academic and administrative services.
Despite these advances, ITS faces ongoing constraints related to staffing levels.
These constraints limit the pace at which new services can be expanded, legacy systems modernized, and emerging risks addressed.
As a result, certain enhancements in areas su ch as advanced security operations, expanded user support, and broader adoption of emerging technologies may require phased implementation over multiple years.
Through targeted investments and strategic partnerships, ITS supports student learning, faculty research, and institutional operations while managing risk and aligning technology capabilities with available resources and long-term University priorities.

FACILITIES The University’s current physical plant of 5. 7 million square feet across four campuses consists of 3 22 buildings (including leased buildings) including 24 residence halls, plus three apartment complexes and two dining centers, as well as the Memorial Union’s Ram’s Den.
Throughout its nearly continuous building program, the University has been successful in obtaining public financial support through the approval of bonds of the State issued for the benefit of the University for both renovation of older buildings and the construction of new buildings.
Over the last ten years, the University has completed more than $550 million in new construction and renovation and rehabilitation of existing structures.
Recent Completed Construction and Major Renovations: 2013 to 2024 Robert J.
Higgins Welcome Center.
September 26, 2018 marked the official opening of the $8.2 million Robert J.
Higgins Welcome Center, funded by generous donors and one -time University funding sources.

Located on a prominent site on Upper College Road, this new state of the art building is an important tool for continuing the growth in applications which has enabled the University to increase enrollment significantly over the last ten years in the face of declining numbers of high school graduates nationally and regionally, while simultaneo usly increasing both the quality of the student body and its diversity.
The Higgins Welcome Center showcases URI students and their successes and enhances that all-important first impression for prospective students and families upon arrival at the Kingston Campus.
The Fascitelli Center for Advanced Engineering (College of Engineering Phase I).
On October 7, 2019, the University dedicated The Fascitelli Center for Advanced Engineering, a new 187,000 square foot

A-27 building.
The phase 1 project started with the removal of five buildings that were built in the 1950s and 1960s to clear the site for the construction of the new building as well as renovation of the Kirk building.
The Fascitelli Center, funded by a generous donor as well as general obligation bonds issued by the State, comprises an east and west wing that are connected via what is effectively a truss bridge.
This center bridge manifests its structural members on the façade of the building, giving visual form to the engineering knowledge taught within which is in high demand by major employers in Rhode Island and serves as a draw to the State.
The College of Engineering Phase II project, which opened in January 2020, included the renovation of Bliss Hall and a new 15,000 square foot addition to the building.
This renovation restored the historic façade of Bliss Hall, home to the original College of Engineering when it opened in 1 928 and established a new addition that architecturally linked Bliss Hall to The Fascitelli Center.
These projects were supported collectively by $150.5 million in voter approved general obligation bond support from the State.
Meade Stadium Artificial Turf .

In 2019, the University of Rhode Island Athletic Department in conjunction with the Division of Student Affairs successfully completed the installation of an artificial surface and lights on Meade Stadium.
This project turned a facility that was used only six to eight times a year into one that can be used daily by URI’s varsity football program, along with general student use through intramurals and club sports.
This $4.1 million project, funded through $3 million of generous donor support and one-time Auxiliary Funding, was completed in time for the opening home football game on September 7, 2019.
Brookside Residence Hall.
The Brookside Residence Hall, an apartment-style residence hall on the west bank of the White Horn Brook on the Kingston campus, was dedicated on February 10, 2020.
This project is part of the University’s continuing initiative to provide safe, convenient, and affordable housing on the Kingston campus.
This state-of-the-art residence facility provides 500 new beds in an apartment-style six- story building focusing on upperclassmen.

In addition to providing safe and affordable housin g, working with the Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management, this project restored the section of White Horn Brook from Flagg Road to West Alumni Avenue, providing wildlife habitat, campus amenities, and stormwater improvements for this area of campus.
As an added amenity to the students living in Brookside and others on campus, this project provided the final northern connection to the campus bike path.
This bike path is now complete from Flagg Road heading south for approximately two miles to connect with the eight-mile William C.
O'Neill Bike Path that leads from the historic Kingston train station to the beaches in Narragansett.
Ranger Hall Phase II.
The Ranger Hall Phase II renovation was completed in August 2022.
This project built on the success of phase one, which opened in the fall of 2016 with the expansion of the Harrington School of Communication and Media to the second, third, and fourth floors of this historic building on the Kingston campus.

This renovation of the upper floors of Ranger Hall, funded by a generous private gift, provides the Harrington School with high technology classroom space to advance the Harrington School of Communication and Media as well as much needed general assignment classrooms in the heart of the academic core of the campus.
Soloviev Basketball Practice Facility.
In the fall of 2023, the University completed an $8.0 million privately fundraised renovation of the Soloviev Basketball Practice Facility.
This facility provides 24-hour access to state -of-the-art training facilities for URI’s highly competitive men's an d women's basketball programs.
Infrastructure.
In the 2018 legislative session $19.8 million of much needed paving ($11 million), infrastructure ($6.5 million) and auxiliary fire protection ($2.3 million) projects were approved for revenue bond financing.
Working with RIHEBC these bonds have been issued in support of further improvements

A-28 of the campus’ hardscape, infrastructure and life safety needs.
To date $22.6 million (including interest and additional bond proceeds) has been expended out of these bond sources.
Phase Three of the University's progressive efforts to repave and reconstruct major parking facilities, internal roadways, walkways, and drainage systems across three of its four campuses has been completed.
The University has upgraded the high voltage electrical substations and electrical infrastructure on the Kingston Campus.
Work was completed on a new substation at Butterfield Road and an expanded substation on Flagg Road.
Improvements were made to the existing electrical system to support flexible back -feed capability throughout the system.
In 2024, the university began the installation of a centralized "generator farm" at the intersection of Butterfield and West Alumni Avenue to service the Roger Williams Complex residential buildings, and also conduct critical repairs to the steam line underneath the Hammerschlag Mall.
In addition, in 2023, Phase 2 of our Utility bond strategy was initiated.

In June of 2023, a bond for $15.44 million was issued and work has begun to improve our utility infrastructure systems on campus with this funding.
To date, we have spent $12.4 million.
Projects in Progress Narragansett Bay Campus Renewal – Phase I.
Leading an East Coast Oceanographic Consortium, the University of Rhode Island’s Graduate School of Oceanography in 2018 secured the management contract for a new, $125 million National Science Foundation (NSF) Regional Class Research Vessel, the Narraganset Dawn.
This vessel’s home base will be URI’s Narragansett Bay Campus.
To support this and other cutting-edge research that is ongoing at the Narragansett Bay Campus, in November 2018, Rhode Island voters approved $45 million of general obligation bonds of the State to support the project.
Phase IA of this project is the construction of a new, larger pier for the NSF research vessel.
The pier is substantially complete.Phase 1B of this project is to deliver the Ocean Robotics Laboratory, which will be completed in April 2026.
This building will bring together faculty from the Graduate School of Oceanography and the Ocean Engineering department.

Equipment and robotics pioneered here will work hand -in-glove with the new Regional Class Research Vessel, Narragansett Dawn, and its advanced overboard -handling systems for launch and recovery of scientific equipment at sea.
Moreover, the 33,000 square-foot facility will create opportunities for collaborations within URI, among university partners and through public-private ventures.
Narragansett Bay Campus Renewal – Phase II.
In November 2022, Rhode Island voters approved the issuance of $100 million in State of Rhode Island general obligation bonds to support the second phase of the renewal of the Narragansett Bay Campus including the replacement of the antiquated buildings housing the Graduate School of Oceanography (“GSO”) and Ocean Engineering (“OE”).
The State has also contributed $25 million in RICAP dollars in support of the project.
The GSO generates over $32 million in grant activity each year and this project will allow them to grow that capacity by as much as 150%.
OE is a leader in the State’s efforts to capture clean energy.

The replacement of the Ocean Engineering Complex will provide the ability for OE to continue to lead the State forward in the development of Rhode Island’s Blue Economy as URI continues to lead these efforts toward economic growth in this important sector.
Fine Arts Center Renovation .
In the 2020 session the legislature approved the referendum for $57.3 million in general obligation bonds to go before State voters to recapitalize the Fine Arts Center.
State voters generously approved the bond as part of a special election in March 2021.
This project will remove two antiquated building pods from the complex renovate three building pods and construct a new three - story building to provide new space for the Art, Theater and Music departments.
Construction on the Fine Arts Center is underway and will complete in the Spring of 2026.
Water Filtration Plant.
At the end of the Fiscal Year 2022 legislative session, the Rhode Island General Assembly enacted legislation that establishes a concentration limit of 20 parts per trillion of Per - and Polyfluorinated Substances (“PFAS”) in public drinking water supplies.
The legislation established the Rhode Island Department of Health as the regulatory body for monitoring compliance with this new

A-29 standard.
The Environmental Protection Agency in March 2023 has similarly proposed to establish legally enforceable levels for six PFAS known to occur in drinking water, and this proposed rule is currently out for comment.
The University, which is licensed as a municipal -level water system subject to the newly enacted Rhode Island law, received $20 million in RICAP funds support from the state of Rhode Island to design and construct a water system filtration plant.
As of November 2024, the first phase of construction of the filtration plant was completed with that phase 1 effort successfully supplying “PFAS-free” water to the campus.
Next steps include completing design efforts for Phase 2 of the filtration plant that expands the plants capabilities and extends the useful life of the plant for the next 20-30 years.
The university anticipates awarding a design -build-operate contract in 2026, with intended phase 2 completion by fiscal year -end 2027.
Capital Maintenance.
During the 2022 legislative session, URI secured its highest ever commitment from the State in RICAP support.

By appropriating close to $140 million in RICAP, the State has shown that it is committed to the ongoing improvements and preservation of the campus infrastructure and buildings that support the ongoing work to educate tomorrow’s workforce and develop new technologies to drive the future of the Rhode Island economy.
RICAP funds are “pay -as-you-go” State surplus funds dedicated to capital maintenance which enable the State to reduce the amount of debt – and thus expense - incurred for this purpose.
Phase three of the University’s Utility Improvement project was also approved in the 202 5 legislative session.
This phase of utility improvements will focus on the replacement or upgrade of major University utility systems.
Student Housing.
URI is moving forward with a plan to construct additional housing on the Kingston Campus that will provide more than 1,100 additional beds for undergraduate and graduate students on the Kingston Campus.
Gilbane Development Company has been selected as the University’s development partner in a new public -private partnership.

Partnering with a private developer represents an innovative approach to housing more students on campus in University-supervised buildings.
The project has achieved financial close and is currently in construction for both undergraduate buildings.
Graduate Village will commence construction in June 2026.
The two phases will complete in the summer of 2027 and the summer of 2028.
ENTERPRISE RISK MANAGEMENT The University has instituted an Enterprise Risk Management (“ERM”) program.
ERM is the formal and systematic effort to control the impact of uncertainty and variability on an organization’s strategic objectives by managing risks at all levels of the organization.
ERM differs from traditional risk management by taking a holistic approach to managing risk.
As part of the ERM program, the University procures appropriate insurance as one of many risk control and mitigation measures.
The University is insured for various risks of loss arising out of claims for negligence, including bodily injury and property damage, wrongful acts, cyber liability, professional liability and workers compensation through a combination of insurance polici es and self -insurance.

The University’s property insurance program covers University buildings and contents against risks of dire ct physical loss, on a blanket, replacement cost basis.
As of Jan 2026, total property value for the University’s four campuses is reported as $2.3 billion.
There is a $250,000 deductible per building for damage caused by a Named Windstorm and a $200,000 deductible for any other peril on an aggregated basis.
Total property coverage is $240,000,000.
PUBLIC SAFETY Fostering a safe and secure environment for those who live, learn, work and visit is paramount at the University.
The Department of Public Safety supports the University with a sworn police department, office

A-30 of emergency management, emergency dispatch and communications, fire and life safety, alarm services, transportation and parking services, and administration division.
The URI Police Department is responsible for and has jurisdiction over all URI campuses and is staffed by sworn University Police Officers and non -sworn campus patrol persons.
The department patrols on the Kingston campus 24/7 and respond to calls for service at all satellite campuses including the Narragansett Bay Campus and Rhode Island Nursing Education Center (RINEC) in Providence.
The Office of Emergency Management provides planning and services for preparedness, response, recovery, prevention and mitigation and serves as the liaison with other local, state, and federal emergency providers and responders.
Transportation and Parking provides safe, sustainable, reliable, and cost-effective transportation and parking services that facilitate convenient access to the University by students, faculty, staff, and visitors.
Our key services include providing campus transportation shuttles, utilizing patrols and technology to enforce parking regul ations, and promoting more sustainable transportation options.

Transportation and Parking operates a comprehensive shuttle system managed by the University using a private v endor.
The service is widely used by students living both on and off -campus, as well as faculty and staff.
In addition, the Rhody Safe Rides service provides late -night on -demand rides to enhance student security.
The Transportation and Parking Office uses technology which streamlines the purchase of parking permits for a better customer experience and increased efficiency.
Throughout the year, new and returning students and all community members receive print, web, video and email information and training about resources available to protect them against injury, fire and other threats and to ensure that the University continu es its mission in a safe, secure, and inclusive environment.
URI Public Safety takes a community policing approach to their work, and the URI Police are an integral part of the daily life of the University.

President DATE: June 15, 2026 SUBJECT: Action Item: Approval of the FY2028―FY2032 Capital Improvement Plan Purpose of Submittal: The University is seeking approval from the University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees for the submission of the University of Rhode Island FY2028―FY2032 Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) to the State of Rhode Island, which the committee reviewed at its April meeting.
The CIP, due in July of each year, is the first FY28 budget submittal in the cycle and is a five-year rolling plan of proposed University capital projects of $1.0M or greater, using unrestricted funds together with related requests for State funding.
Points to Consider: The enclosed presentation provides updates to existing CIP projects' scope/budget/schedule, including the Narragansett Bay Campus Phase 2, the Athletics Complex Renewal, the Biomedical Sciences Building, Student Success, and the Public Safety Building.

It also provides information for the Memorial Union and Health and Counseling Center projects, which are both now scheduled for reactivation following our successful P3 Housing project outcome.
The presentation also highlights several projects, with a heavy emphasis on addressing the significant backlog of asset renewal needed on URI’s buildings, which in total comprise 28% of the State’s buildings.
These additions include the refurbishment of the Carothers Library HVAC systems , the university’s water tower , Allen Harbor bulkhead and dock replacement, and the NBC shoreline stabilization project.
Two new projects are proposed to be added to the CIP this year : including a new Graduate School of Oceanography (GSO) Marine Operations Building, including renovations to the Aquarium Ark, to support the new R/V NARRAGANSETT DAWN, and the renovation of the Middleton building on the NBC to provide spaces for the GSO Marine Geological Samples Laboratory and the Facilities.
The CIP also recommends a 2028 General Obligation (GO) Bond project for Student Success.

Although currently envisioned as a standalone facility on the site of the Carlotti Building, we will investigate the opportunity to move this program into the Carothers’ Library as we reenvision how the library is best used to support the ongoing needs of our campus community.

Recommendation: I recommend that the Board of Trustees approve the enclosed University of Rhode Island Capital Improvement Plan for FY2028―FY2032. Supporting Information: Please see University of Rhode Island FY 2028- FY2032 CIP Enclosure. Proposed Motion of the Board: THAT, the Board of Trustees approve the University of Rhode Island Capital Improvement Plan for FY2028- FY2032 as presented.

President DATE: April 13, 2026 SUBJECT: Action Item: Approval of the demolition of the Sheets Building, Horn Laboratory, and Center for Atmospheric Chemistry Studies on the Narragansett Bay Campus Purpose of Submittal: The University is seeking approval from the University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees to demolish three buildings at the Narragansett Bay Campus as part of the Narragansett Bay Phase Two Renewal project.
The three buildings are the Sheets building at 15 Receiving Road, Horn Laboratory (Horn) at 29 Fish Road, and Center for Atmospheric Chemistry Studies (CACS) at 8 Reactor Road , all of which are located on Plat N -C, Lot 7 in the Town of Narragansett.
Points to Consider: Demolition of all three buildings is required as part of the Narragansett Bay Phase Two Renewal project.

The footprint of the Sheets building will be replaced by the new Ocean Engineering Complex; a new Ocean Frontiers Building will accommodate the programs from Horn and CACS and be located twenty feet from the footprint of Horn.
Recommendation: I recommend that the University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees approve the demolition of all three buildings to allow for the advancement of the Narragansett Bay Phase Two project.
This recommendation is based on a thorough review by the appropriate stakeholders and working in conjunction with Ellenzweig, the architects for the project.
Supporting Information: Please see the attached presentation slide.
Proposed Motion of the Board: To recommend approval to demolish the Sheets Building, Horn Laboratory, and the Center for Atmospheric Chemistry Studies located on Plat N-C, Lot 7 in the Town of Narragansett, Rhode Island.

TO: The University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees, Finance and Facilities Sub-committee FROM: Marc B.
Parlange, Ph.D., P.Eng., President DATE: February 2, 2026 SUBJECT: Discussion Item: Review of the Governor’s FY2027 Recommended Budget Purpose of Submittal: To provide an overview of the Governor’s FY27 recommended budget (GRB ).
The GRB includes recommendations on URI’s operating budget and capital requests for consideration by the General Assembly during the legislative session.
Points to Consider: Operating: • URI’s FY2 7 operating budget request included $3.8M to address the operating shortfall, $23.6M to address current service level needs, and $ 10.2M in strategic initiatives.
The GRB recommended $0 to address the operating shortfall, $4.2M in support of our current service level, and $0 in support of strategic initiatives.
Of the $4.2M increase in current service level, $1.3M is designated for increased centralized charges from the State, including for the RI ERP system.
Capital: • URI’s FY27 capital request included $17.3M in RICAP Asset Protection funds.

The GRB recommended $15.2M. • URI’s FY27 capital request included $16.5M in RICAP to address accessibility-related projects.
The GRB recommended $ 9.0M, which includes suggested ongoing funding beyond FY31 at FY31 levels ($1M/year). • URI’s FY27 capital request included $53M in RICAP to address building envelope projects.
The GRB recommended $21M, which includes suggested ongoing funding beyond FY31 at FY31 levels ($3M/year). • The URI FY27 capital request included $1.575M for RICAP to support access control at URI.
The GRB recommended the full $1.575M. • The GRB recommended funding for several other capital projects were in line with previous appropriations, including the PFAS water treatment plant, the Athletic Complex Renewal, Narragansett Bay Campus improvements, the Fine Arts Center, Academic Fire Protection, and Stormwater Management. • URI RICAP r equests for Carothers HVAC ($67.6 M), Allen Harbor Bulkhead & Dock replacement ($6.7M), and Public Safety Building ($48.3M) were not recommended for funding in the GRB.

TO: The University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees, Finance and Facilities Committee FROM: Marc B.
Parlange, Ph.D., P.Eng., President DATE: February 2, 2026 SUBJECT: Action Item: Consideration of a Resolution on Bond Reimbursement Purpose of Submittal: The University is seeking approval from the Board of Trustees for a resolution allowing for the reimbursement of expenditures related to two infrastructure projects that may be made by the University prior to the issuance of debt supporting these projects.
The University anticipates seeking authorization from the Board to issue a revenue bond in fall 2026 to support both projects.
The proposed reimbursement amount would be capped at $6.91M, which equals the portion of the project costs anticipated to be spent between now and bond issuance, with a 15% contingency buffer.
